newsitem.title: UK: Crude down in expectation of higher US oil stocks.
newsitem.headline: Crude down in expectation of higher US oil stocks.

text.p: World oil prices edged lower on Tuesday for a seventh consecutive day of losses as expectations of a further recovery in U.S. heating oil stocks outweighed concerns over heart surgery on Russian leader Boris Yeltsin.
Many players were keeping to the sidelines ahead of key U.S. oil and product data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) due out after the close.
But expectations of a build in heating oil stocks as a result of record refinery output overturned earlier market gains.
London December Brent crude futures finished down 10 cents a barrel at $22.18.

With about a third of Russia's 6.2 million barrels a day output exported outside the old Soviet Union, dealers expressed concern that if surgery on Yeltsin's heart failed Russia could be plunged into political turmoil.
But London traders largely played down the "Yeltsin factor", particularly as a surgeon monitoring the president's treatment hailed the multiple heart bypass as a "complete success."
"I don't think Yeltsin's operation was much of a factor," said Christopher Bellew of brokers Prudential-Bache. "In fact we read that it's been a success anyway."
"No great alterations to energy policy will take place even if the Presidency changes," said brokers GNI in a market review.
Traders also put Tuesday's action down to a temporary technical correction which some suggested may not last for long.
"Overall the trend is distinctly downwards," Bellew said.

Crude values raced to a near-six-year post-Gulf War high of $25.06 in mid-October, fuelled by fears of low heating oil stocks in the run-up to the peak winter demand period combined with tensions in the Middle East.
But mild weather, rising U.S. heating oil inventories and investment fund selling helped dampen bullish sentiment.
While the short term outlook for oil remained bearish, few in the market expected substantial losses ahead of the traditional peak demand period.

"Both Europe and the U.S. are currently experiencing mild weather, but once temperatures fall, the focus should return to the distillate shortfall, which could support prices all winter if maintained," GNI said.

Traders noted that delegates to the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and analysts were predicting the group's output ceiling would remain unchanged when OPEC ministers meet at the end of the month in Vienna.
But it came as no surprise to the market.
"It's bound to (remain unchanged)," Bellew said.
